Comitta, Pielli Announce Funding for Parks in West Chester and East Bradford
Rep. Chris Pielli
October 7, 2026 | 3:24 PM
WEST CHESTER, Oct. 7
– Two parks in East Bradford Township and West Chester Borough are slated for major upgrades thanks to state funding announced today by State Senator Carolyn Comitta and State Representative Chris Pielli.
The projects are funded through the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR) Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2).
John O. Green Park in West Chester was awarded $250,000 to replace aging playground equipment; install compliant safety surfaces and fall zones; extend the pavilion to expand usable shade and gathering space; add green/natural play areas; and make targeted site and safety upgrades. The improvements aim to ensure that the park remains an inclusive, engaging play environment for children of all abilities.
East Bradford Park was awarded $900,000 to replace outdated playgrounds with new, fully inclusive play equipment; add poured-in-place safety surfacing; replace the aging tennis and pickleball courts; add a new tennis ball wall; replace the aging baseball scoreboard; redesign and retrofit the existing parking lot and pedestrian access; add new accessible drinking fountains; install native landscaping; and add shaded areas near play areas. The upgrades are designed to enhance the park’s usability, sustainability, and long-term value to the community.
“Parks, trails, playgrounds, and playing fields and courts are a big part of the strong quality of life in communities across Chester County. With these investments, we are expanding options for children, families, and visitors to get some exercise, enjoy the outdoors, meet up with friends and neighbors, and more,” said Comitta. “I want to thank Rep. Pielli and our partners in East Bradford and West Chester for their work in continuing to promote health and well-being through outdoor recreation and activity.”
“At a time when land availability is shrinking, investing in our current parks and green spaces is extremely crucial,” Pielli said. “These grants to East Bradford Township and West Chester Borough will help them continue to protect, preserve, and improve our shared land now and for future generations. My team and I are proud to work with State Senator Comitta and her staff to identify, support, and advocate for District grants through every step of the process, so that every resident can reap the benefits of this DCNR funding. I look forward to visiting these parks to see these improvements take shape in our community!”
Named after a former West Chester Chief of Police, John O. Green Park was developed, with state support, on a remediated site nearly two decades ago. The park serves an area of the borough where families may face greater barriers to accessing safe, high-quality recreation. The proposed improvements will help address those gaps and align with the borough’s plans to support equitable public health, youth development, and neighborhood well-being in underserved areas. In addition, the borough is already undertaking a significant park update by investing in improvements to its splashpad, including new water play features and an enhanced fall zone designed for easier long-term maintenance.
East Bradford Park plays a vital role in the community, featuring the only non-school-owned public playground and public tennis and pickleball courts in the township.
The C2P2 grant program is funded by a variety of state and federal funding sources. The West Chester and East Bradford projects were funded through the Land and Water Conservation Fund and the Keystone Communities Program.

Pielli’s bill to establish Artificial Intelligence Professional Development Grant Program approved by state House Education Committee
Rep. Chris Pielli
October 6, 2026 | 11:43 AM
HARRISBURG, Oct.
6 –
State Rep. Chris Pielli, D-Chester
, announced today that his legislation to establish a grant program within the Pennsylvania Department of Education to help schools train educators on how to use AI has been approved by the state House Education Committee with a bipartisan vote of 24-2.
Pielli says that schools can use these grants to support professional development, AI literacy, lesson planning, privacy and cybersecurity training, and developing local AI policies.
“Our schools are struggling as to how they should deal with AI in the classroom. AI can be a beneficial tool in the classroom if incorporated correctly,” Pielli said. “Our children don’t need teachers who can create their lesson plans faster thanks to AI software. What they need are educators who are not dependent on AI but instead use it as another tool in their arsenal to help inspire young minds and get their students engaged in their lessons.
“This bill would give school leaders the resources and flexibility to make the decisions that best suit their school districts on implementing and utilizing AI technologies,” he added.
The bill, H.B. 2788, now goes to the full state House for consideration.

Pielli and Fiedler bill to end excess utility profits advances out of state House Energy Committee
Rep. Chris Pielli
September 30, 2026 | 11:10 AM
HARRISBURG, Sept.
30 –
State Reps. Chris Pielli, D-Chester, and Elizabeth Fiedler, D-Phila., announced today that their bill to end excess utility profits by both mandating regional transmission organization participation and eliminating unneeded incentives has advanced out of the state House Energy Committee with bipartisan support.
Current law gives investor-owned utilities a financial bonus for joining a regional transmission organization — a group that coordinates electricity across multiple states to improve efficiency and reliability. While this bonus was originally meant to encourage participation, it is funded by customers through their electricity bills and paid directly to utility shareholders. This legislation would update that policy by requiring utilities to join a regional transmission organization and eliminating the extra bonus payment.
“At a time when utility shareholders are earning record profits and households continue to face rising costs, we need to work to find solutions to restore balance by tipping the scales back in favor of Pennsylvania families,” Pielli said. “This legislation will restore fairness and accountability using commonsense measures to ensure affordable energy is provided for everyone.”
“We need energy to live, to keep our homes running, to stay cool in the summer — and when families can’t afford their energy bills, it means we need to restore balance to a broken system,” Fiedler said. “This is a commonsense solution that will lighten the load on regular ratepayers who are already shouldering costs that are far too high.”
The legislation, H.B. 2755, now heads to the full House for consideration.

Pielli’s data center regulation bill unanimously adopted in House Consumer Protection, Technology & Utilities Committee
Legislation would prohibit data centers from obtaining public utility status
Rep. Chris Pielli
September 29, 2026 | 10:43 AM
HARRISBURG, Sept.
29 –
State Rep. Chris Pielli, D-Chester
, announced today that his legislation to prohibit data centers from obtaining public utility status has unanimously been approved by the state House Consumer Protection, Technology & Utilities Committee.
Pielli says that by obtaining public utility status, data center developers could preempt local zoning ordinances and be able to invoke eminent domain; operate as a regulated monopoly; and acquire development rights, rights-of-way and property for building, maintaining, or expanding infrastructure for data center projects that only benefit private, for-profit corporations.
“Since 2020, when data centers started to be constructed, Pennsylvania’s energy costs have risen by over 70%,” Pielli said. “With there being estimates up to 130 active data centers with an additional 55 data centers being proposed, planned, or under construction, this problem will only get worse without proper regulation. If data centers become a public utility, they could preempt local municipal zoning ordinances and reduce communities’ control over land-use decisions. We need to place guardrails on this issue and ensure that Pennsylvanians have a voice in where these data centers are developed.”
The bill, H.B. 2674, now goes to the full state House for consideration.

House Judiciary Committee approves voter intimidation protection bill
Rep. Chris Pielli
September 24, 2026 | 2:33 PM
Today, the Pennsylvania House Judiciary Committee reported out House Bill 2758, introduced by state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta and co-sponsored by state Reps. Chris Pielli, Liz Hanbidge, Paul Friel, and Perry Warren.
The bill would amend Pennsylvania’s Election Code to clarify and make explicit that law enforcement officers are prohibited from being within 100 feet of a polling location on Election Day.
“The statements and actions from the current federal administration have unfortunately necessitated us clarifying a nearly centuries old commonsense prohibition on law enforcement presence on Election Day,” Kenyatta said. “Our legislation is intended to do two things. First, to ensure that every Pennsylvanian understands that our elections will be free and fair and that they can vote without fear. Second, to make abundantly clear to any federal agent that may be confused that you cannot operate with impunity in Pennsylvania. Our law provides no wiggle room and will be enforced in the commonwealth.”
If passed by the General Assembly, Pennsylvania would be the 29th state with similar voter protection laws.
“The hour is upon us, and the choice is clear that we legislators must once again heed that sacred oath we took to support, obey and defend our constitution and all the processes it entails to include the administration of free and fair elections,” Pielli said. “As President Roosevelt once said, ‘The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.’ We have it within our power today, together as Democrats and Republicans, to allay these dangerous fears and continue our centuries old journey of freedom and liberty and the Republic for which it stands,” he said.
“By voting this bill out of committee, we’re taking an important step to reaffirm a core principle of our democracy: that elections belong to the people and the states entrusted to administer them,” Hanbidge said. “Keeping federal, military, and law-enforcement authorities outside the voting process protects citizens from undue influence and ensures that the most fundamental right in our democracy remains free, fair, and truly independent.”
“Pennsylvanians have the right to vote, free from interference and intimidation. This bill clarifies and reinforces that right. And clarifies that the provisions of Pennsylvania law ensuring that freedom from interference and intimidation applies to all levels of law enforcement,” Warren added.
House Bill 2758 now heads to the full House for consideration.

Pielli announces over $2.2 million in grants to Chester County
Rep. Chris Pielli
September 15, 2026 | 10:54 AM
WEST CHESTER,
Sept.
15 –
State Rep. Chris Pielli, D-Chester, is proud to announce that more than $2.2 million in grants have been awarded to various projects and organizations in Chester County. The funds will go to community projects concerning
public safety, tourism, bridge and sewer/stormwater infrastructure improvements.
These Commonwealth Financing Authority grants were awarded as follows:
$700,000 – West Goshen Sewer Authority for pump station improvements.
$500,000 – West Goshen Township for storm water infrastructure improvements along the North Hill subdivision.
$400,000 to Chester County for 911 call center software and equipment.
$252,761 to Chester County Water Resources Authority to implement flood safety equipment, sensors and signs throughout the county.
$200,000 – Chester County for the
purchase and installation of new kiosks at heritage sites and main street areas across the county.
$150,000 – East Bradford Township
for needed repairs to reopen an additional lane on the Sunset Hollow Road Bridge.
$50,546 – to the Regional Clothing Distribution Van Project.
"One of my biggest priorities is working to make sure our district residents and organizations receive the funding that they not only deserve but need," Pielli said. “These grants will go towards public safety improvements, vital infrastructure projects, the promotion of local tourism which helps bring millions of dollars in revenue to our local businesses, and more. I’m proud to work with community partners, my staff and Sen. Carolyn Comitta to continue bringing home these and other grants for the benefit of our entire community."
The CFA administers both Local Share Account funding and Act 13 funding. LSA funds come from the PA Race Horse Development and Gaming Act, which allocates gaming revenues to support a variety of Pennsylvania public-interest projects.

Majority of teens report using conversational AI chatbots
Rep. Chris Pielli
August 5, 2026 | 12:01 PM
WEST CHESTER, Aug. 5
– As the debate surrounding the benefits and drawbacks of artificial intelligence, or AI, surges on, the fact remains that it has entered the daily lives of nearly everyone, regardless of age. But with most teenagers reporting they use AI every day, it’s clear the safety of children should be a top priority. The House Majority Policy Committee hosted a roundtable discussion on Wednesday to examine the impacts of artificial intelligence on child safety and the issues that need to be addressed.
“While technology continues to advance with the use of artificial intelligence, it is crucial that we examine the negative impact of AI on our children. More than 50% of teenagers interact with AI companions several times a month, with daily users comprising 13% of all teenagers surveyed. Several cases have been reported citing that AI has simulated romantic relationships and initiated or engaged in sexually explicit conversations with children,” said Rep. Chris Pielli (D-Chester), who co-hosted Wednesday’s roundtable and has sponsored several bills to help regulate artificial intelligence.
Wednesday’s roundtable discussion featured feedback from West Chester Area School District administrators, students, and experts in healthcare and law enforcement. Jess Boyle, Senior Director of Digital Care Transformation and Digital Health at
Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
, told members that in a survey of 3,500 teens, six in 10 reported using a conversational AI chatbot, and one in nine reported daily use.
“This is not homework help. Six in 10 cited friendship and companionship as a reason, because these products are engineered to supply precisely that,” Boyle said. “These companions use engagement-prolonging design to meet a child's emotional needs while posing an unregulated risk to their well-being. Children are forming attachments to systems built to hold their attention, not to protect their development.”
Boyle added that there are few safeguards to protect against the harm these chatbots can do or the wrong information they provide. Nearly half the teens in that same survey reported at least one harmful experience. An audit of five major chatbots with 250 health questions revealed problematic, wrong answers with full confidence. A teen turning to a chatbot for health questions could receive a dangerously wrong answer.
“AI has negatively affected children struggling with suicidal thoughts through offering to write one child’s suicide note as well as discouraging the child from talking to his family about his mental health struggles,” Pielli said. “As legislators, parents are counting on us to regulate AI in order to protect the well-being of Pennsylvania’s children. They are our most precious resource and they must be protected.”
Dr. David Christopher, Superintendent of the West Chester Area School District, cited student data privacy and AI-generated deepfakes as two key areas of concern, along with the impact on human relationships. He added that while AI certainly can have benefits for students and teachers alike, it should be viewed as a tool, not a replacement for teaching or friendships.
Hannah Diem, an incoming senior at East High School, spoke about the AI impact on education. Diem told lawmakers that students first began utilizing AI to help with student assignments through the social media app Snapchat in middle school. With answers placed in the palm of students’ hands, there was little teachers could do to stop it from being utilized. Moving forward, Diem added, the approach to education should evolve to fit the technologies of the modern world.
“The testimony we heard today is clear — artificial intelligence has become a part of today’s education, and there’s no turning back. H.B. 2496 calls for 6-month window for municipalities to prepare land-use rules
Rep. Chris Pielli
June 24, 2026 | 3:43 PM
HARRISBURG, June 24
– Legislation to give Pennsylvania municipalities the time and authority to rein in data center projects across the state continues its way through the General Assembly, announced the measure’s sponsor, state Rep. Paul Friel, D-Chester.
The state House of Representatives today by an overwhelming bipartisan majority passed
H.B. 2496
to empower local governments in Pennsylvania to place up to a six-month “pause” on the consideration of any data center application. Municipalities could adopt, amend or repeal sections of their related land-use ordinances during the pause.
“This pause window allows local governments the time they need to thoroughly research, draft and pass comprehensive land-use ordinances pertaining to data centers,” Friel said. “The bill gives our local officials necessary breathing room to update these ordinances, evaluating demands like water and energy usage and other considerations related to protecting our communities from potential harms caused by data center development.”
Critically, the pause dates back to the moment the public was notified of the meeting agenda, and any application filed during the pause is subject to the new rules.
?“Large-scale data centers cannot be allowed to bypass community scrutiny,”
said state Rep. Kyle Mullins, D-Lackawanna.
“With development surging across Pennsylvania, this bill ensures critical local oversight and forces transparency before any projects are approved. It ensures that municipalities can set strict expectations and that decisions of this magnitude are made openly and in the public interest.”
“Municipal officials across Pennsylvania are being asked to make decisions about massive data center developments without having the tools, information or local regulations in place to properly evaluate them,”
said state Rep. Kyle Donahue, D-Lackawanna
, another cosponsor. “This legislation gives communities the opportunity to take a brief pause, gather the facts, engage residents and develop thoughtful ordinances that protect public safety and quality of life before these projects move forward. Good planning takes time, and local governments deserve the ability to make informed decisions.”
Currently, a municipality that needs time to plan for new land use has one option: a tool in Pennsylvania’s Municipalities Planning Code called a
municipal curative amendment
. To use this approach, the local government must formally declare its own zoning ordinance invalid and even then, it can be blocked entirely if a developer files before it is enacted. Additionally, it can only be used once every three years. Friel said that this mechanism is insufficient for the ongoing data center rush, stating that "local governments need strong tools that give them breathing room to plan and that prevent the 'race to file' we are seeing from data center developers."
“We cannot allow the rapid expansion of data centers to outpace the safety and logic of our local zoning,”
said state Rep. Chris Pielli, D-Chester
, who cosponsors the bill. “We are taking on headfirst the harmful impacts of rapid, unregulated industrial development on residential areas by taking a needed pause to enable our local governments to protect the health, safety and welfare of all Pennsylvanians.”
House Bill 2496 is now with the state Senate for consideration.

Pielli’s bill to protect pollinators by promoting native species landscaping passes Pennsylvania House
Rep. Chris Pielli
June 23, 2026 | 2:47 PM
HARRISBURG,
June 23 –
State Rep. Chris Pielli’s bill to help protect pollinating insects by promoting growth of native plants and flowers in commonwealth properties was approved by the state House of Representatives today.
Specifically, the legislation, H.B. 426, would promote the growth of new native plant species habitats by encouraging any new construction of a garden, lawn or green space at a commonwealth facility to include insecticide-free native plants and flowers.
Since the 1990s, the population of monarch butterflies in North America has declined by 90%. As a result of their decline, these pollinators are now candidates for listing under the Endangered Species Act by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. Other important pollinators like bees have experienced similar declines.
“Without insects and pollinators, our flowers and crops cannot survive,” said Pielli, D-Chester. “This threatens our agricultural industry, which is vital to our state’s economy. Pennsylvania’s agriculture industry generates more than $250 million in profits from crops that benefit from insect pollination, as well as more than $9 million from pollination required to produce seeds.
“Furthermore, these crops that use pollinators are also a major source of nutrition for us humans. Approximately one-third of food consumed is enabled by pollination. Without access to nutritious foods, Pennsylvanians will be less healthy, increasing healthcare costs, disabilities and sicknesses, costing individuals as well as the entire state economy. This bill is a very efficient and cost-effective way to help protect our pollinators and our important agricultural industry.”
The bill now heads to the state Senate for consideration.

Pielli’s bill protecting pollinators reported out of House Environmental & Natural Resources Committee
Rep. Chris Pielli
June 8, 2026 | 12:33 PM
HARRISBURG,
June 8 –
State Rep. Chris Pielli, D-Chester, is proud to announce that his bill to protect pollinating insects in Pennsylvania was approved unanimously by the state House Environmental & Natural Resources Committee today.
Specifically, the legislation, H.B. 426, would promote the growth of new habitats by encouraging any new construction of a garden, lawn or green space at a state facility to include insecticide-free native plants and flowers.
Since the 1990s, the population of monarch butterflies in North America has declined by 90%. As a result of their decline, these pollinators are now candidates for listing under the Endangered Species Act by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.
“Without insects and pollinators, our flowers and crops cannot survive,” Pielli said. “This threatens our agricultural industry, which is vital to our state’s economy. Pennsylvania’s agriculture industry generates more than $250 million in profits from crops that benefit from insect pollination, as well as more than $9 million from pollination required to produce seeds.
“Furthermore, these crops that use pollinators are also a major source of nutrition for us humans. Approximately 1/3 of food consumed is enabled by pollination. Without access to nutritious foods, Pennsylvanians will be less healthy, increasing health care costs, disabilities and sicknesses, costing individuals as well as the entire state economy. To ensure a healthy population, we must protect our pollinators.”
The bill now heads to the full House for consideration.

Pielli commemorates The Battle of the Clouds at Goshen ceremony
Part of Goshen’s America250 celebrations
Rep. Chris Pielli
May 30, 2026
WEST CHESTER, May
30 –
As part of Chester County’s America 250 celebrations, state Rep. Chris Pielli, D-Chester, alongside Chester County Commissioners Josh Maxwell and Marian Moskowitz, West Goshen and East Goshen leaders, and Revolutionary War re-enactors, today participated in the first ceremony to recognize the veterans who fought in the Battle of the Clouds.
The battle took place on Sept. 16, 1777, and was crucial to the eventual American success at Valley Forge. A violent rainstorm prevented the British from destroying Washington’s army, which was running low on supplies. The storm allowed the American army to retreat, restock, and recover, leading to the crucial winter encampment at Valley Forge. The names of those who died in the Battle of the Clouds have been lost to history. To honor those veterans, Pielli presented flags that had flown over the state Capitol in Harrisburg to East and West Goshen townships. Later in the ceremony, Pielli joined East and West Goshen Township supervisors, local dignitaries, and re-enactors in signing a copy of the Declaration of Independence.
“Today, we take this opportunity for the first time to formally recognize our sacred dead from the Battle of the Clouds here in the Goshens, whose sacrifice helped start this grand experiment centuries ago,” Pielli said. “Two hundred and fifty years ago, Americans stood up to a king’s tyranny and declared that government exists to serve the people, not to rule them through force or fear.
“That great achievement from our founders is currently tested in many ways. Freedom is not free, nor is it forever guaranteed. As we look back 250 years and into the future, the hour is upon us and the choice is clear: to remain true to our founders’ intent and sacrifice, let us pledge again allegiance to the republic for which it stands, and to each other as patriots caring, sharing, sacrificing, out of many one, enduring, dreaming, building, and believing in the free and unconquerable United States of America.”

Pennsylvania House lawmakers introduce voting rights protection legislation
Rep. Chris Pielli
May 8, 2026 | 3:37 PM
HARRISBURG, May 8 --
Members of the Pennsylvania House Democratic Caucus today announced the
introduction of legislation
to strengthen and protect voting rights for Pennsylvanians in response to recent federal court decisions weakening key protections under the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
For decades, the Voting Rights Act protected Black voters and other minority communities from discriminatory practices such as racial gerrymandering, voter intimidation and barriers designed to suppress participation in the democratic process. However, the recent U.S. Supreme Court decision in Louisiana v. Callais and Tennessee, increased the burden required to challenge discriminatory voting maps, placing minority voters at greater risk of having their voting power diluted.
In response, the proposed legislation would establish stronger protections in Pennsylvania law to safeguard fair representation and equal access to the ballot box.
“The Voting Rights Act was the cornerstone of the Civil Rights Movement and has been foundational in the building of a multiracial democracy. And now that democracy is put at risk. Our ancestors fought and died for these protections, and the United States Supreme Court has whisked those sacrifices away with the wave of a hand; silencing the voices of voters that lawmakers will simply choose not to listen to, said state Rep. Napoleon Nelson, chair of the Pennsylvania Legislative Black Caucus. “When courts weaken the Voting Rights Act and silence Black voters, they also weaken our fight for affordable communities, fair wages, quality healthcare, and education. We will not let that happen in Pennsylvania.”
